results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, et al.
results.key_finding: Empiric antibiotic regimen for adults older than 50 years, alcoholics, or immunocompromised patients: ampicillin 2g IV every 4 hours PLUS ceftriaxone 2g IV every 12 hours PLUS vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV every 8-12 hours. Ampicillin is added specifically to provide coverage for Listeria monocytogenes, which is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins. Adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 days is recommended, given before or with the first antibiotic dose.
results.title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis

results.authors: Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D.
results.key_finding: Listeria monocytogenes accounts for approximately 7-8% of adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis. Risk groups include adults older than 50 years, immunocompromised patients (organ transplant, corticosteroids, HIV), and pregnant women. Rhombencephalitis — involvement of the brainstem and cerebellum — occurs in a distinct subset of Listeria CNS infections and may present with cranial nerve palsies, ataxia, and altered consciousness. CSF findings are often less typical than pneumococcal meningitis: Gram stain sensitivity is approximately 33% (compared to 70-90% for pneumococcus), and a lymphocytic or mixed pleocytosis may be seen. Treatment of choice is ampicillin; cephalosporins are inactive.
results.title: Community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults

results.authors: van de Beek D, Cabellos C, Dzupova O, et al.
results.key_finding: In suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis in patients older than 60 years or with immune compromise, empiric regimens must include ampicillin alongside ceftriaxone and vancomycin because Listeria monocytogenes is not covered by cephalosporins. CSF Gram stain has low sensitivity (~33%) in Listeria meningitis; a negative Gram stain in an elderly or immunocompromised host must not exclude Listeria coverage.
results.title: ESCMID guideline for diagnosis and treatment of acute bacterial meningitis

output.summary: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis disproportionately affects elderly patients (age >50), immunocompromised individuals (corticosteroids, malignancy, HIV, transplant), and pregnant women. Empiric regimens for these risk groups must include ampicillin 2g IV every 4 hours, as Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; ceftriaxone or cefotaxime alone would leave Listeria uncovered. CSF Gram stain sensitivity for Listeria is approximately 33%, substantially lower than for pneumococcus, and a negative Gram stain must not be used to exclude Listeria coverage in at-risk hosts. Rhombencephalitis is a recognized complication of CNS Listeria infection, manifesting with brainstem and cerebellar signs; MRI is superior to CT for detection. Adjunctive dexamethasone is given per standard bacterial meningitis guidelines, though evidence specifically for Listeria is limited.

key_clinical_evidence: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis disproportionately affects adults aged >50, immunocompromised hosts (corticosteroids, diabetes, malignancy, transplant), and pregnant women; age >71 on chronic prednisone with diabetes is a classic risk profile.

CSF Gram stain sensitivity for Listeria is approximately 33% — far lower than for Streptococcus pneumoniae (~70-90%) — so a negative Gram stain does not exclude Listeria and must not be used to withhold ampicillin in an at-risk host.

The CSF pleocytosis in Listeria meningitis is often mixed (neutrophilic-lymphocytic) rather than the classic PMN-dominant pattern of pneumococcal meningitis; this atypical pattern anchors a naive clinician toward viral meningitis.

Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins; standard empiric regimens omitting ampicillin (vancomycin + ceftriaxone alone) provide NO Listeria coverage and must be expanded in any patient aged >50 or immunocompromised.

Rhombencephalitis — brainstem and cerebellar involvement — is a recognized manifestation of CNS Listeria infection; cranial nerve palsies (particularly abducens, facial) and ataxia reflect dorsal pontine involvement and should prompt MRI and Listeria-inclusive empiric therapy.

The posterior-circulation stroke mimic (abducens palsy + pontine MRI signal) must be actively excluded by DWI (no restriction here) and integration with the infectious syndrome before narrowing to a vascular diagnosis.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Eduardo Castellanos is a 71-year-old right-handed man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and rheumatoid arthritis on chronic low-dose prednisone who presents to the emergency department brought by his wife for a three-day history of worsening headache, low-grade fever, and progressive confusion. His wife reports that three days ago he began complaining of a bifrontal headache he described as a pressure-like sensation, worse in the morning and not relieved by acetaminophen. The following morning his temperature was 37.9°C and he appeared generally unwell, refusing breakfast. He was seen at an urgent care center that afternoon and told he likely had a viral illness; no antibiotics were prescribed. Over the next 24 hours his headache intensified and he developed nausea with two episodes of non-bloody vomiting. He was intermittently confused, repeating questions and unable to recall the correct day. His wife noted he seemed unsteady reaching for objects with his left hand and had a mild tremor when trying to write. This morning she noticed that his left eye appeared to be 'not moving all the way to the left,' prompting her to call emergency services. In the ED, Mr. Castellanos is lethargic but responds to his name. He reports severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. He denies any recent sick contacts, head trauma, or prior episodes. His wife confirms he has been eating soft cheeses and deli meat sandwiches regularly over the past few weeks. He has received no recent antibiotics. His diabetes has been poorly controlled recently, and he has been on prednisone 7.5 mg daily for three years without interruption. He is not on any prophylactic antibiotics or antifungals. He has not received meningococcal or pneumococcal vaccines in the past 5 years.
